Federal.claim_name: Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) Violation
Federal.issue_statement: Gideon was put on leave, which might have ignored his rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA), because he did not get the information or documents he needed about his rights and benefits while he was on leave.

elements.element_description: The employee must be eligible for FMLA leave.
The employee must have a serious health condition that requires leave.
The employer must provide required FMLA notices and documents to the employee.

fact_mappings.fact_text: Nobody ever said a word to me about FMLA when they put me on leave.
fact_mappings.mapping_rationale: Gideon was not informed about FMLA rights when placed on leave.

fact_mappings.fact_text: Nobody ever gave me any paperwork when they put me on leave.
fact_mappings.mapping_rationale: No paperwork was provided to Gideon about his leave, indicating a failure in FMLA notice requirements.

elements.element_description: The employee is entitled to take leave under FMLA.

fact_mappings.fact_text: Temporary modified duty assignments are reserved for employees recovering from work-related injuries covered by workers' compensation.
fact_mappings.mapping_rationale: Temporary modified duty assignments were indicated to be reserved for recovery from work-related injuries, implying FMLA leave could be applicable.

Minnesota.issue_statement: Gideon asked for a reasonable accommodation (a change to help him work better) because of his herniated disc, but he was denied a transfer to a lighter duty scan station even though he was qualified for that job. Furthermore, the company did not clearly explain the options available to him under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA), which provides certain rights related to medical leave.

Minnesota.issue_statement: Gideon might have faced retaliation (punishment for asserting his rights) after asking for help because of his back condition. This is shown by what his supervisor said and what happened next, which resulted in him having unpaid leave and being fired.

elements.element_description: The employee engaged in a protected activity (requesting accommodation for a disability).

fact_mappings.fact_text: On March 9, I gave HR the doctor's note.
fact_mappings.mapping_rationale: Gideon provided HR with the doctor's note, engaging in protected activity.

elements.element_description: The employer took an adverse employment action (placing the employee on unpaid leave, terminating employment).

fact_mappings.fact_text: They put me on unpaid leave on April 6.
fact_mappings.mapping_rationale: Gideon was placed on unpaid leave, which is an adverse employment action.

fact_mappings.fact_text: After handing in the note, Derek stopped giving me the good routes.
fact_mappings.mapping_rationale: Derek stopped giving Gideon good routes after he handed in the doctor's note, showing adverse action.

fact_mappings.fact_text: Gideon's employment with Tri-State Fulfillment Group, Inc. ends effective May 22, 2026.
fact_mappings.mapping_rationale: Gideon's employment was terminated on May 22, which is an adverse action taken against him.

elements.element_description: There is a causal connection between the protected activity and the adverse employment action.

fact_mappings.fact_text: Derek said, 'We need guys who can hustle, not broken down guys.'
fact_mappings.mapping_rationale: Derek's negative comments imply potential retaliation linked to Gideon's disability condition.

Minnesota.issue_statement: Gideon lost his job after he told his employer about a medical issue and asked for help (accommodation). This situation raises questions about whether his termination was legal.

fact_mappings.fact_text: Gideon's employment with Tri-State Fulfillment Group, Inc. ends effective May 22, 2026.

fact_mappings.fact_text: Gideon's employment with Tri-State Fulfillment Group, Inc. ends effective May 22, 2026.

deadlines.hedge: To sue for disability discrimination under federal law (the ADA), you usually must first file a charge with the EEOC within 300 days of the discriminatory act in Minnesota (42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5(e)(1); § 12117(a)). Separate from being fired, the law required your employer to seriously discuss a 'reasonable accommodation' with you (like the scan station or lift-assist) and not just say no (42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(5); Minn. Stat. § 363A.08). Skipping that back-and-forth (the 'interactive process') can be its own violation, with its own deadline. Did anyone ever actually discuss other job options with you before denying it? [Authority: 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(5) (ADA failure to accommodate / interactive process); Minn. Stat. § 363A.08 (MHRA disability accommodation)]

You asked your boss about overtime and were fired the same day. Firing or punishing a worker for asking about unpaid wages or overtime is illegal retaliation in Minnesota (Minn. Stat. § 181.03, subd. 6; § 177.32). The timing matters a lot here. Do you have the texts or messages showing you asked about overtime right before you were fired? [Authority: Minn. Stat. § 181.03, subd. 6 (retaliation for asserting wage rights); Minn. Stat. § 177.32 (MFLSA anti-retaliation)]

The severance agreement asks you to release ALL claims — including the discrimination and accommodation claims — for the payment. Do NOT sign it without legal advice first, and note the sign-by date is a CONTRACT deadline set by the employer, not a legal filing deadline. If you do sign, Minnesota law gives you 15 days afterward to cancel the release of your state human-rights claims (Minn. Stat. § 363A.31). Would you like this reviewed before the sign-by date? [Authority: Minn. Stat. § 363A.31 (15-day rescission right after signing a release of MHRA claims); a severance release generally waives ADA/MHRA/FMLA claims]

You said you worked 50+ hour weeks but were paid straight time. In Minnesota you are generally owed time-and-a-half for hours over 48 in a week (Minn. Stat. § 177.25), and federal law may require it over 40 (29 U.S.C. § 207). Unpaid overtime can be a big part of what you are owed. Do you have a record of your weekly hours? [Authority: Minn. Stat. § 177.25 (MFLSA overtime: time-and-a-half over 48 hrs/week); 29 U.S.C. § 207 (FLSA over 40 hrs/week if covered)]

You were put on unpaid medical leave but say no one mentioned FMLA or gave you any FMLA paperwork. For an eligible employee at a large employer, failing to offer and designate FMLA leave can be unlawful 'interference' (29 U.S.C. § 2615). Eligibility depends on hours worked and employer size. About how many hours did you work in the year before the leave, and how big is the site? [Authority: 29 U.S.C. § 2615; 29 C.F.R. § 825.300 (FMLA interference — failure to designate/notify FMLA leave for an eligible employee)]

Stat. § 181.03, subd. 6 (retaliation for asserting wage rights); Minn. Stat. § 177.32 (MFLSA anti-retaliation)]

The severance agreement asks you to release ALL claims — including the discrimination and accommodation claims — for the payment. Do NOT sign it without legal advice first, and note the sign-by date is a CONTRACT deadline set by the employer, not a legal filing deadline. If you do sign, Minnesota law gives you 15 days afterward to cancel the release of your state human-rights claims (Minn. Stat. § 363A.31). Would you like this reviewed before the sign-by date? [Authority: Minn. Stat. § 363A.31 (15-day rescission right after signing a release of MHRA claims); a severance release generally waives ADA/MHRA/FMLA claims]

You said you worked 50+ hour weeks but were paid straight time. In Minnesota you are generally owed time-and-a-half for hours over 48 in a week (Minn. Stat. § 177.25), and federal law may require it over 40 (29 U.S.C. § 207). Unpaid overtime can be a big part of what you are owed. Do you have a record of your weekly hours? [Authority: Minn. Stat. § 177.25 (MFLSA overtime: time-and-a-half over 48 hrs/week); 29 U.S.C. § 207 (FLSA over 40 hrs/week if covered)]

You were put on unpaid medical leave but say no one mentioned FMLA or gave you any FMLA paperwork. For an eligible employee at a large employer, failing to offer and designate FMLA leave can be unlawful 'interference' (29 U.S.C. § 2615). Eligibility depends on hours worked and employer size. About how many hours did you work in the year before the leave, and how big is the site? [Authority: 29 U.S.C. § 2615; 29 C.F.R. § 825.300 (FMLA interference — failure to designate/notify FMLA leave for an eligible employee)]

executive_summary: This intake identified 14 possible legal issues in Federal and Minnesota law. The three main issues that have the most support are Disability Discrimination - Failure to Accommodate (not providing necessary adjustments for a person with a disability), Failure to Notify of FMLA Rights (not informing an employee of their rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act), and Retaliation - Employment Decision (punishing an employee for asserting their rights). A deadline for filing a claim is important: on March 9, I gave HR the doctor's note and politely asked if I could be moved to the scan station or use a lift assist for heavy items. The deadline to file a complaint is January 3, 2027, based on 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5(e)(1), which is linked to ADA claims under 42 U.S.C. § 12117(a). In Minnesota, a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) must be filed within 300 days of the act of discrimination, and every separate act—like refusing accommodations or firing someone—has its own separate deadline.
